lesson.title: The Telegram That Backfired: Germany's Offer to Mexico
lesson.summary: In January 1917, Germany secretly proposed a military alliance with Mexico against the United States, offering to help Mexico reclaim Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, but British codebreakers intercepted the message, and its publication pushed American opinion decisively toward war.
lesson.body:
By early 1917, German military leaders had decided to gamble. They planned to resume unrestricted submarine warfare, meaning German U-boats would sink any ship, including unarmed merchant and passenger vessels, approaching Britain or its allies without warning. German planners understood this policy risked provoking the United States into entering the war on the side of the Allies described in the previous chapter, but they were betting they could starve Britain into surrender before American troops could arrive in meaningful numbers. To hedge against that risk, German Foreign Secretary Arthur Zimmermann tried to arrange a distraction closer to American shores.

On January 16, 1917, Zimmermann sent a coded telegram to the German minister in Mexico. The message proposed that if the United States entered the war against Germany, Mexico should ally itself with Germany instead. In exchange, Germany promised to help Mexico reconquer the territory it had lost to the United States in the Mexican-American War of the 1840s, meaning Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona. The telegram also suggested that Mexico try to persuade Japan to join this new alliance against the United States.

What Zimmermann did not know was that British naval intelligence, working out of a codebreaking unit known as Room 40, had already intercepted and decoded the telegram. British officials carefully passed the contents to the American government in late February 1917, while taking pains to disguise exactly how they had broken the German code, so as not to reveal their intelligence methods. The telegram was published in American newspapers on March 1, 1917. After initial disbelief, Zimmermann himself publicly confirmed its authenticity just days later.

The reaction across the United States was outrage. A public already unsettled by German submarine attacks now confronted a documented German scheme to help Mexico seize American territory. Combined with the resumption of unrestricted submarine warfare, the Zimmermann Telegram dramatically shifted American public opinion toward supporting entry into the war, setting the stage for the events covered in the next chapter, just weeks later.
